<section class="lmx-band"><div class="lmx-wrap"><div class="lmx-split">
<figure class="lmx-photo lmx-rv"><img src="/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/68c07e14071307565ffa9f5f_mentor-1536x1024.jpg" srcset="/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/68c07e14071307565ffa9f5f_mentor-768x512.jpg 768w, /wp-content/uploads/2025/12/68c07e14071307565ffa9f5f_mentor-1024x683.jpg 1024w, /wp-content/uploads/2025/12/68c07e14071307565ffa9f5f_mentor-1536x1024.jpg 1536w, /wp-content/uploads/2025/12/68c07e14071307565ffa9f5f_mentor-2048x1365.jpg 2048w" sizes="auto, (min-width:960px) 600px, 100vw" width="2560" height="1707" alt="Two people reading through a book together at a table" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
<figcaption class="lmx-float"><b>A planning tool for families</b><span>Not medical advice. Care decisions belong with his treatment team.</span></figcaption></figure>
<div class="lmx-rv">
<p class="lmx-eyebrow">Why it matters</p>
<h2>Why the first 90 days matter</h2>
<div class="lmx-prose"><p>Finishing treatment is a real milestone. It’s also the point where the structure of a program ends and ordinary life starts again: work or school, money, old friends, free time. Many families find these first months harder than they expected, not because treatment failed, but because staying sober in daily life is a different skill from getting sober in a program.</p>
<p>This guide is a planning tool for families. It isn’t medical advice. Decisions about medical or mental health care belong with your son’s treatment team and his own doctors.</p></div>
</div>
</div></div></section>

<section class="lmx-band lmx-bleed lmx-alt" id="lmx-before" style="scroll-margin-top:110px"><div class="lmx-wrap">
<div class="lmx-rv">
<p class="lmx-eyebrow">Before discharge</p>
<h2>The two weeks that matter most</h2>
<p class="lmx-intro">Start planning before the discharge date, not after. Ask the treatment team:</p>
</div>
<div class="lmx-grid2 lmx-rv">
<div class="lmx-step"><span class="lmx-step-n">1</span><div><p style="margin:4px 0 0;color:#eef1f8">What do you recommend as the next step, and why?</p></div></div>
<div class="lmx-step"><span class="lmx-step-n">2</span><div><p style="margin:4px 0 0;color:#eef1f8">Does he need ongoing outpatient care, therapy or medication follow-up? Who will provide it, and are appointments already booked?</p></div></div>
<div class="lmx-step"><span class="lmx-step-n">3</span><div><p style="margin:4px 0 0;color:#eef1f8">What level of structure do you think he needs right now?</p></div></div>
<div class="lmx-step"><span class="lmx-step-n">4</span><div><p style="margin:4px 0 0;color:#eef1f8">What warning signs should we watch for, and who do we call if we see them?</p></div></div>
</div>
<div class="lmx-rv" style="margin-top:56px">
<h3 style="font-size:1.45rem">Where will he live?</h3>
<p class="lmx-intro" style="margin:0">Then talk together as a family about where he’ll live. The main options are:</p>
<div class="lmx-tablecard"><div class="lmx-tablewrap"><table class="lmx-table"><thead><tr><th>Option</th><th>What it offers</th><th>What to think about</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Coming home</td><td>Familiar surroundings, family support</td><td>Less structure; old routines and contacts are close by</td></tr>
<tr><td>Sober living</td><td>Substance-free housing, house expectations, peers in recovery</td><td>Not treatment; usually private pay</td></tr>
<tr><td>Structured sober living</td><td>More daily structure and accountability</td><td>Asks more of residents; often a minimum stay</td></tr>
<tr><td>Continued clinical care (outpatient or residential)</td><td>Ongoing treatment</td><td>Decided by the treatment team</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div></div>
<div class="lmx-note"><p>There isn’t one right answer for everyone. A useful question is: <em>how much structure does he need right now to practice the habits he built in treatment?</em></p></div>
</div>
</div></section>

<section class="lmx-band"><div class="lmx-wrap">
<div class="lmx-rv">
<p class="lmx-eyebrow">The first 90 days</p>
<h2>What to expect, month by month</h2>
</div>
<div class="lmx-tl">
<div class="lmx-phase lmx-rv"><span class="lmx-days">Days 1–30</span><h3>Settling in</h3><p>The first month is about routine. Whatever the living situation, aim for:</p>
<ul class="lmx-list"><li>A predictable daily schedule: waking up, meals, work or school, meetings, sleep</li><li>Every outside appointment kept (therapy, outpatient, medical)</li><li>Regular contact with a recovery community, such as 12-step or other mutual-help meetings</li><li>Clear expectations agreed in advance, so they don’t have to be negotiated every day</li></ul>
<div class="lmx-fam"><b>What families can do</b>Keep contact steady and calm. Ask how he’s doing, not only whether he’s sober. Resist the urge to manage every detail.</div></div>
<div class="lmx-phase lmx-rv"><span class="lmx-days">Days 31–60</span><h3>Building responsibility</h3><p>As routines settle, responsibility can grow:</p>
<ul class="lmx-list"><li>Work, school or volunteering becomes a regular part of the week</li><li>He handles more of his own money, appointments and transport</li><li>He starts repairing relationships at a pace that works for everyone</li></ul>
<div class="lmx-fam"><b>What families can do</b>Notice effort, not just results. Hold the agreements you made, even when it’s uncomfortable. If you’re paying for things, decide together what he’ll take over and when.</div></div>
<div class="lmx-phase lmx-rv"><span class="lmx-days">Days 61–90</span><h3>Looking ahead</h3><p>By the third month, many people start thinking about what comes next: more independence, a new job, a different living situation.</p>
<ul class="lmx-list"><li>Is he keeping his routines without reminders?</li><li>Is he handling setbacks without disappearing or going back to old habits?</li><li>Does he still have people around him who are sober and honest with him?</li></ul>
<div class="lmx-fam"><b>Remember</b>Moving on should follow steady behavior, not a date on the calendar.</div></div>
</div>
</div></section>

<section class="lmx-band lmx-bleed lmx-alt"><div class="lmx-wrap">
<div class="lmx-grid2" style="margin-top:0">
<div class="lmx-card lmx-rv"><div class="lmx-ico">✓</div><h3>Talking about boundaries and money</h3><p>Boundaries work best when they’re specific, agreed in advance and kept. For example:</p>
<ul class="lmx-list"><li>What you’ll pay for, what he’ll pay for, and when that changes</li><li>What happens if he drinks or uses</li><li>How often you’ll be in touch, and how</li></ul>
<p style="margin:14px 0 0">Write them down. Revisit them at day 30 and day 60.</p></div>
<div class="lmx-card lmx-card--amber lmx-rv"><div class="lmx-ico">!</div><h3>Warning signs to take seriously</h3><p>Contact his treatment team or a medical professional if you notice:</p>
<ul class="lmx-list"><li>Missed appointments or meetings, or dropping his support network</li><li>Secrecy about money, time or friends</li><li>Big changes in sleep, mood or eating</li><li>Talk of hopelessness or not wanting to be here</li></ul></div>
</div>
<div class="lmx-crisis lmx-rv"><span class="lmx-crisis-i">!</span><p>If you’re worried about his immediate safety, call <b>911</b>. For a mental health or suicidal crisis, call or text <b>988</b> (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline). For free, confidential treatment referrals, call SAMHSA’s National Helpline at <b>1-800-662-HELP (4357)</b>, 24/7.</p></div>
<div class="lmx-note lmx-rv"><p><strong style="color:#fff;display:block;font-family:var(--disp);font-size:1.15rem;margin-bottom:6px">A relapse doesn’t erase progress</strong>If he drinks or uses, act quickly and calmly. Contact his treatment team, follow the plan you agreed, and focus on the next right step rather than blame.</p></div>
</div></section>

<section class="lmx-band"><div class="lmx-wrap">
<div class="lmx-rv">
<p class="lmx-eyebrow">Where sober living fits</p>
<h2>A place to practice, while recovery is still new</h2>
<div class="lmx-prose"><p>Sober living gives someone a substance-free place to practice work, routines and accountability while recovery is still new. It isn’t right for everyone, and it isn’t a substitute for clinical care when that’s needed.</p>
<p>Ethos Recovery is a non-clinical sober living community for men in Los Angeles, with three levels of support: the Ethos Flagship Program, Ethos Recovery Apartments in Culver City, and Ethos Transitional Living in West Adams. Ethos doesn’t provide detox, therapy or medical treatment; residents who need those services receive them from outside providers.</p></div>
<div class="lmx-facts"><span class="lmx-fact"><b>Ethos Flagship Program</b></span><span class="lmx-fact"><b>Ethos Recovery Apartments</b> · Culver City</span><span class="lmx-fact"><b>Ethos Transitional Living</b> · West Adams</span></div>
</div>
</div></section>

<section class="lmx-band lmx-bleed lmx-alt" id="lmx-checklist"><div class="lmx-wrap">

<p class="lmx-eyebrow">Your plan</p>
<h2>Your 90-day planning checklist</h2>
<p class="lmx-intro">Tick items off as you go. Your progress stays in your browser.</p>
</div>

<li><label><input type="checkbox" value="5"><span>Boundaries and money agreements written down</span></label></li>

</ul>

</div></section>

<section class="lmx-hero lmx-bleed"><img class="lmx-hero-img" src="/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65ca71b8ebbc2a47e4896396_IMG_9683-1536x1024.jpeg" srcset="/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65ca71b8ebbc2a47e4896396_IMG_9683-768x512.jpeg 768w, /wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65ca71b8ebbc2a47e4896396_IMG_9683-1024x683.jpeg 1024w, /wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65ca71b8ebbc2a47e4896396_IMG_9683-1536x1024.jpeg 1536w, /wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65ca71b8ebbc2a47e4896396_IMG_9683-2048x1365.jpeg 2048w, /wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65ca71b8ebbc2a47e4896396_IMG_9683-scaled.jpeg 2560w" sizes="100vw" width="2560" height="1707" alt="Two smiling young men hugging outdoors among trees" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"><div class="lmx-hero-shade"></div><div class="lmx-wrap lmx-hero-in"><div class="lmx-hero-copy"><p class="lmx-kicker"><span class="lmx-dot"></span>Free guide for families</p><h1 class="lmx-h1">A Guide to <em>Sober Living</em></h1><p class="lmx-hero-lead">What it is, how it works, and how to choose the right home.</p><div class="lmx-actions"><a class="lmx-btn" href="#what-sober-living-is">Start reading <span class="lmx-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><a class="lmx-btn lmx-btn--ghost" href="#lmx-copy">Get a copy by email</a></div><ul class="lmx-trust"><li>9 short chapters</li><li>Plain-language comparisons</li><li>How to choose a home</li><li>Free, no sign-up to read</li></ul></div></div></section>
<section class="lmx-band"><div class="lmx-wrap"><div class="lmx-doc"><aside class="lmx-toc"><p>Contents</p><ol><li><a href="#what-sober-living-is">What sober living is</a></li><li><a href="#who-sober-living-is-for">Who sober living is for</a></li><li><a href="#how-sober-living-works-day-to-day">How sober living works day to day</a></li><li><a href="#sober-living-rehab-halfway-houses-and-transitional-living">Sober living, rehab, halfway houses and transitional living</a></li><li><a href="#how-long-people-stay">How long people stay</a></li><li><a href="#how-to-choose-a-home">How to choose a home</a></li><li><a href="#cost-and-who-pays">Cost and who pays</a></li><li><a href="#supporting-someone-in-sober-living">Supporting someone in sober living</a></li><li><a href="#sober-living-at-ethos">Sober living at Ethos</a></li></ol></aside><div class="lmx-chaps"><section class="lmx-chap" id="what-sober-living-is"><span class="lmx-chapn">01</span><h2>What sober living is</h2><p>Sober living is substance-free housing where people in recovery live together, follow house expectations, and practice the routines of everyday life without drugs or alcohol. It isn’t clinical treatment. Residents usually work, go to school or volunteer, attend recovery meetings, and help run the house. Many people move into sober living after detox or treatment, when they need more support than home can offer.</p></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="who-sober-living-is-for"><span class="lmx-chapn">02</span><h2>Who sober living is for</h2><p>Sober living tends to fit people who:</p><ul class="lmx-list"><li>Have finished detox or treatment, or are medically stable</li><li>Want to stay sober but don’t yet have the structure or support to do it at home</li><li>Are ready to work, study or volunteer and share responsibility for a house</li></ul><div class="lmx-note"><p>It may not be the right fit for someone who needs medical or psychiatric care around the clock. That decision belongs with a treatment team.</p></div></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="how-sober-living-works-day-to-day"><span class="lmx-chapn">03</span><h2>How sober living works day to day</h2><p>Most homes share a few basics:</p><div class="lmx-grid2" style="margin-top:18px"><div class="lmx-card"><h3>House expectations</h3><p style="margin:0">Sobriety, chores, curfews, meetings, respect for housemates</p></div><div class="lmx-card"><h3>Accountability</h3><p style="margin:0">Drug testing and regular check-ins</p></div><div class="lmx-card"><h3>Routine</h3><p style="margin:0">Work, school or volunteering during the day; meetings and house time in the evening</p></div><div class="lmx-card"><h3>Community</h3><p style="margin:0">Living with others in recovery who notice when something is off</p></div></div><figure class="lmx-inimg"><img src="/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65bce1a4266d60cb795c8e20_IMG_3926-1536x1024.jpg" srcset="/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65bce1a4266d60cb795c8e20_IMG_3926-768x512.jpg 768w, /wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65bce1a4266d60cb795c8e20_IMG_3926-1024x683.jpg 1024w, /wp-content/uploads/2026/03/65bce1a4266d60cb795c8e20_IMG_3926-1536x1024.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (min-width:1024px) 800px, 100vw" width="2560" height="1707" alt="A tidy shared bedroom with bunk beds at an Ethos home" loading="lazy" decoding="async"></figure><p style="margin-top:18px">The point isn’t to keep someone dependent on structure. It’s to practice stability until he can carry more responsibility on his own.</p></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="sober-living-rehab-halfway-houses-and-transitional-living"><span class="lmx-chapn">04</span><h2>Sober living, rehab, halfway houses and transitional living</h2><div class="lmx-tablecard" style="margin-top:8px"><div class="lmx-tablewrap"><table class="lmx-table"><thead><tr><th> </th><th>Sober living</th><th>Rehab (residential treatment)</th><th>Halfway house</th><th>Transitional living</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>What it is</td><td>Substance-free housing with peer support</td><td>Clinical treatment program</td><td>Often a step from incarceration or treatment, sometimes court-related</td><td>A step toward fully independent living</td></tr><tr><td>Clinical care on site</td><td>No</td><td>Yes</td><td>Varies</td><td>No</td></tr><tr><td>Daily freedom</td><td>Moderate</td><td>Low</td><td>Varies</td><td>Higher</td></tr><tr><td>Who pays</td><td>Usually private pay</td><td>Often insurance</td><td>Varies</td><td>Usually private pay</td></tr></tbody></table></div></div><p style="margin-top:22px">Transitional living is a step between a structured recovery setting and fully independent living. Residents stay in a sober, supportive environment but have more say over their schedules, work and daily decisions.</p></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="how-long-people-stay"><span class="lmx-chapn">05</span><h2>How long people stay</h2><p>There isn’t one length of stay that works for everyone. The more useful question is whether the person can keep up recovery, work, relationships and daily routines with less outside structure. Many homes set a minimum stay; the Ethos structured community asks for a minimum commitment of three months. Moving on should follow steady behavior, not a date on the calendar.</p></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="how-to-choose-a-home"><span class="lmx-chapn">06</span><h2>How to choose a home</h2><p>Look for clear house expectations, regular drug testing, a real plan for how residents spend their days, and staff who can explain how they handle relapse and conflict. Ask how long residents usually stay, what the fee includes, and whether the home is certified by a recognized recovery-residence organization. A well-run home should answer these questions plainly.</p><div class="lmx-note"><p>Our free checklist, <a href="/sober-living-questions-checklist/">Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Sober Living Home</a>, has the full list to bring to every call and every tour.</p></div><div class="lmx-actions" style="margin-top:18px"><a class="lmx-btn" href="/sober-living-questions-checklist/">Open the free scorecard <span class="lmx-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span></a></div></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="cost-and-who-pays"><span class="lmx-chapn">07</span><h2>Cost and who pays</h2><p>Sober living is usually private pay. It’s housing and peer support rather than medical treatment, so rent is typically paid by the resident or family. Health insurance may still cover clinical care someone receives while living in sober housing, such as outpatient treatment, therapy or psychiatric appointments with outside providers. Ask each home exactly what its monthly fee includes before committing.</p></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="supporting-someone-in-sober-living"><span class="lmx-chapn">08</span><h2>Supporting someone in sober living</h2><ul class="lmx-checks" style="margin-top:8px"><li><label style="cursor:default"><span>Agree on expectations before move-in: money, contact, what happens after a relapse</span></label></li><li><label style="cursor:default"><span>Keep contact steady, and let the house do its job</span></label></li><li><label style="cursor:default"><span>Notice effort and consistency, not just milestones</span></label></li><li><label style="cursor:default"><span>Look after yourself too: family support groups can help</span></label></li></ul></section>
<section class="lmx-chap" id="sober-living-at-ethos"><span class="lmx-chapn">09</span><h2>Sober living at Ethos</h2><p>Ethos Recovery is a structured sober living community for men in Los Angeles. We offer three levels of support:</p><div class="lmx-grid3" style="margin-top:18px"><div class="lmx-level lmx-level--top"><span class="lmx-loc">Los Angeles</span><h3>Ethos Flagship Program</h3><p style="color:#c9cfdd;margin:0">Our most structured level, built around daily routines, 12-step involvement, peer accountability and the R.I.S.E. <details><summary>How is the score calculated?</summary><p>Each of the 30 questions is worth up to 2 points: 2 for a clear answer, 1 for a vague answer, 0 for no answer. They’re shown separately because each one is worth taking seriously on its own.</p></details>
